title: Selling on your own or with a broker

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
« Why pay a commission if I can sell on my own? » The question is legitimate, and deserves a real calculation rather than a slogan. Selling it yourself can suit some people; for others, a broker's support brings in more than it costs.

This guide honestly compares the two options: what a broker really does, the real costs and risks of going « without an intermediary », and how to decide based on your situation.

Each chapter ends with a lined « My notes » page to help you do YOUR calculation.

chapters.title: What a broker really does
chapters.objective: See the full work behind the commission.
chapters.html:
See the full work behind the commission.

  • Set the fair price (comparative analysis) and advise on strategy.
  • Prepare, photograph and market (Centris, broker network, wide distribution).
  • Screen buyers, organize and manage showings.
  • Negotiate offers and conditions in your interest.
  • Oversee the legal aspects (forms, seller's declaration, deadlines) and secure the transaction through to the notary.

The commission pays for all of this work AND the network of buyers it gives access to.

Emilie's tip

The real question isn't « how much does a broker cost? » but « how much do they earn me, net, after commission? ». A better sale price and a secure transaction often more than make up for the fees.

chapters.title: The costs and risks of going « without an intermediary »
chapters.objective: Assess what « selling on your own » really involves.
chapters.html:
Assess what « selling on your own » really involves.

Selling on your own is neither free nor risk-free: the platform package, buying your own services (photos, appraisal), the time invested, and above all the risk of costly mistakes.

  • Risk of mispricing (too high: it lingers; too low: a dead loss).
  • Often less exposure to the network of brokers and their buyers.
  • Direct negotiation, without an intermediary, often emotional.
  • Legal risks: latent defects, a poorly filled-out seller's declaration, post-sale disputes.
Emilie's tip

The most costly mistake in selling on your own is almost always the price: a few percent less on a house is often far more than the commission saved.

chapters.title: The real calculation, figures in hand
chapters.objective: Compare the NET in your pocket in each scenario.
chapters.html:
Compare the NET in your pocket in each scenario.

Compare the NET amount you pocket in each case, not just the commission avoided:

  • Broker scenario: sale price (often optimized) − commission = net A.
  • On-your-own scenario: sale price (it's up to you to reach the right price) − platform and service fees − the value of your time − risk = net B.
  • The difference depends mostly on your ability to get the best price on your own.

Many sellers discover that a good broker gets a higher price that covers their commission — while sparing them the stress and the risk.

Emilie's tip

Do the calculation in net terms, honestly, including the value of your time and the risk of error. It's the only comparison that means anything.

chapters.title: How to decide based on your situation
chapters.objective: Choose the option suited to YOUR case.
chapters.html:
Choose the option suited to YOUR case.

Selling on your own can work if: you know the local market very well, your property is in high demand, you have the time, comfort with negotiation and the rigor for the legal side. Otherwise, a broker's support reduces the risk and aims for a better net result.

There are also in-between formulas (à la carte services). The key: decide with full knowledge, with a real calculation, not a reflex.

Emilie's tip

Meet with a broker before deciding, even if you lean toward « on your own »: at the very least you'll come away with a pricing analysis and a clear view of the market — and often with a better decision.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. List the sale tasks and assess which ones I can take on.
  2. Estimate the value of my time and my comfort with negotiation.

Within 30 days

  1. Do the NET-in-pocket calculation for each scenario.
  2. Meet with a broker to get a pricing analysis.

Next

  1. Decide with full knowledge, figures in hand.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Commission: the broker's fee, paying for all of the sale work.
  • Net in pocket: the amount actually pocketed after all costs.
  • Seller's declaration: a key document to limit latent-defect disputes.
  • À la carte services: in-between formulas between « on your own » and « full service ».
  • Broker network: the pool of buyers accessible through a broker.

options: B) A full body of work and access to a network of buyers
